notes.meaning: Jesus tells His disciples a story about a wealthy landowner whose manager was accused of wasting his property. Like this steward, every person has been given time, money, and gifts that belong to God. We are caretakers of His blessings, not independent owners, and must use them according to His will.

The master calls the manager in to demand his account books and announces that he is being dismissed. In the same way, physical death will one day end our earthly responsibilities. God will then require an account of how we managed everything He placed in our care.

The manager stops to consider his future and realizes he is facing total ruin. He knows he is too weak and unaccustomed to hard farm work to dig ditches, yet he is too proud to beg on the street. He sees that he must act quickly to find a way to survive after his job is gone.

A clever scheme suddenly dawns on the manager to ensure he will not be left homeless. He resolves to do massive favors for the people who owe his master goods. In return, he expects those grateful debtors to welcome him into their homes when he is cast out.

The manager summons his master's debtors one by one to alter their contracts in secret. He tells the first debtor to cut his bill of olive oil in half, and tells the second to reduce his debt of wheat by twenty percent. By using his remaining authority to lower their bills, he buys their goodwill and makes them partners in his scheme.

The master praises the dishonest manager not for his fraud, but for his foresight and clearheaded planning for the future. People of this world often put far more energy, skill, and forethought into their temporal affairs than believers put into their eternal welfare. God's people should be just as thoughtful and eager in pursuing the kingdom of God.

Jesus instructs His followers to use their earthly money, which can so easily mislead people, to do good and show mercy to others. Worldly wealth is temporary and will soon run out when life ends. Those who use money generously to care for God's people will find a joyful welcome waiting for them in eternal dwellings.

A person who shows honesty in small matters will prove honest when trusted with major duties. On the other hand, someone who cheats in tiny things cannot be trusted with greater responsibilities. True faithfulness does not depend on how much we have, but on a sincere desire to honor God in every detail.

Earthly money is temporary, deceptive, and easily lost. It serves as a minor test of our spiritual integrity. If we fail to manage earthly goods according to God's desires, He will not entrust us with genuine, lasting spiritual riches.

Worldly wealth is called another's property because it belongs entirely to God and is only loaned to us for a season. If we prove careless and untrustworthy with what belongs to the Lord, we will not receive heavenly blessings that would be permanently our own. Our handling of material things reveals our fitness for the life to come.

A household servant cannot give wholehearted devotion to two employers who give conflicting commands. In the same way, we cannot divide our ultimate allegiance between the true God and material gain. If money rules our desires, it pushes out love for God.

The Pharisees, who were deeply attached to money, listened to Jesus and openly sneered at His teaching. They felt the sting of His warning against greed and covered their discomfort with mockery. People often ridicule God's truth when it exposes sins they refuse to give up.

Jesus tells the Pharisees that they work hard to appear righteous in front of people, but God sees their hidden thoughts and motives. Human praise often celebrates pride and worldly success, while God detests such hypocrisy. Outward religious acts are worthless before the Lord if the heart remains selfish and greedy.

The era of the Old Testament Law and the Prophets pointed toward the Messiah until John the Baptist arrived to proclaim Him. Now that the good news of God's kingdom is openly preached, people of all kinds are eagerly pressing in to take part in it. Entrance into the kingdom requires earnest spiritual commitment and faith.

The physical universe will pass away before the smallest stroke of a Hebrew letter falls out of God's holy Law. The gospel does not set aside God's moral requirements or make light of His commands. Instead, Jesus confirms the Law's divine authority and brings its promises and moral principles to fulfillment.

Jesus gives marriage as an example of God's unchanging moral standard that people cannot simply alter to suit their desires. He teaches that divorcing a spouse to marry another person violates God's holy institution and results in adultery. God views the marriage bond with far greater seriousness than human customs often do.

differ.view: Some evangelicals believe Jesus' words here strictly forbid all remarriage after divorce without any exceptions.
Many evangelicals believe Jesus gives the general rule here, but permits divorce and remarriage in cases of sexual unfaithfulness or abandonment by an unbelieving spouse.

notes.meaning: Jesus describes a very wealthy man who dressed in royal purple and fine linen, enjoying splendid feasts every single day. He was not charged with open crimes, but he lived only for luxury and personal pleasure. He treated his abundance as his ultimate reward, completely unconcerned about God or eternity.

Just outside the wealthy man's gate lay a destitute beggar named Lazarus whose body was covered with ulcerous sores. Lazarus was physically helpless and had to be carried by others to the entrance in hope of finding food. His condition was as miserable as earthly life could be, yet his name means that God was his only help.

Lazarus longed to satisfy his hunger with the broken bread that fell from the rich man's table, but received no personal care from the owner. Stray street dogs came and licked his open sores as he lay in the dirt. Even wild animals showed the suffering man more pity than his fellow human being did.

The beggar died, and holy angels carried his soul into Abraham's bosom, a picture of honor and resting beside Abraham at the heavenly banquet. The rich man also died and received an elaborate earthly burial. Yet the contrast in eternity proved far greater, as worldly honor ended at the grave while Lazarus entered everlasting joy.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition identifies Abraham's bosom as the limbo of the fathers, where the righteous who died before Christ waited until He opened the gates of heaven.

notes.meaning: The rich man found himself in Hades, the unseen world of the dead, where he was in severe torment. Looking up from his place of misery, he saw Abraham far off and recognized Lazarus resting peacefully beside him. The sight of the poor man's glory deepened the rich man's anguish over the choices he had made.

Suffering terribly in the flame, the rich man cried out to Abraham for pity and begged for Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water to cool his burning tongue. The man who had once refused scraps now begged for a single drop of water. Even in his misery, he still viewed Lazarus as an inferior servant sent to attend to his needs.

Abraham gently calls the man his child according to physical descent, but reminds him that he chose earthly luxuries as his only portion in life. Lazarus had endured deep distress while trusting God, but now their places are completely reversed. Lazarus is comforted forever in the presence of the Lord, while the rich man suffers for living without God.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older critical scholars saw the passage as simply describing a mechanical reversal of fortunes between rich and poor, rather than a moral and spiritual judgment.

notes.meaning: Abraham explains that a vast and unbridgeable chasm has been permanently set between the righteous and the unrighteous. No one in paradise can travel to hell to bring relief, and no one in the place of torment can ever escape to enter heaven. A person's eternal destination is settled at death and cannot be altered.

Realizing his own doom cannot be changed, the rich man begs Abraham to send Lazarus back to earth to visit his father's household. He has five living brothers and wants them urgently warned about the reality of judgment. He knows they are following the very same selfish path that brought him into this place of agony.

Abraham answers that the five brothers already have the books of Moses and the writings of the prophets. The Scriptures contain everything necessary to warn people of judgment, point them to righteousness, and lead them to life. God calls all people to listen to His written word rather than seeking special signs.

The rich man argues back, claiming that his brothers take the Scriptures for granted and will pay no attention to them. He insists that if someone physically returned from the dead to speak to them, they would surely be startled into real repentance. People often wrongly believe that dramatic supernatural events will soften hard hearts when Scripture has failed to do so.

Abraham closes the matter by stating that anyone who refuses to listen to God's written word will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead. Unbelief is a problem of the stubborn human heart, not a lack of miraculous evidence. Genuine faith and lasting repentance come through taking God at His word.
